one_liner: Pure-Swift embeddable WebAssembly interpreter; register-based VM scores 7.5x its old stack interpreter on CoreMark, roughly level with wasm3.
what_it_does: A standalone WebAssembly runtime written in Swift: binary and WAT parser, validator, register-based interpreter, WASI 0.1 and WASI threads, shipped as a SwiftPM library (WasmKit, WasmKitWASI) and the wasmkit-cli tool that Swift 6.2+ toolchains bundle on Linux and macOS. You configure an Engine (threading model, lazy or eager translation, stack size, bounds-check strategy, optional fuel metering), create a thread-confined Store, then instantiate modules and call exports from Swift. It is not a drop-in for wasm3 or wasmi; it is the Swift-native option where a C or Rust runtime is awkward to link.
how_it_is_fast: A single-pass translator turns Wasm stack code into register-machine instructions, after the WAMR fast-interpreter design: 'provider' instructions (local.get, constants) disappear into operand slots of the consuming instruction and local.set is fused into the producer, which matters most for unoptimised (-Onone) Wasm. Dispatch is direct-threaded: each handler is a C function in a header that calls the Swift semantics inline and tail-calls the next handler under the swiftasync (or musttail) convention, with a token-threaded loop as the fallback. The frame layout borrows from the stitch interpreter, and every value occupies a uniform 64-bit slot.
when_to_use: Running Wasm inside a Swift app or server without bundling a C/C++ or Rust runtime and its build system
iOS, tvOS, watchOS, visionOS or other targets where JIT is not allowed, so an interpreter is the only choice
Unoptimised or debug-built Wasm (heavy local.get/const traffic), the case the register design was built for
Embedded Swift and bare-metal targets (an ESP32 example ships), using token threading by default
Tooling that needs WAT parsing, validation, fuel-bounded execution or a GDB remote stub in the same Swift package
when_not_to_use: Throughput-bound workloads where a JIT is allowed: the project's own log shows wasmtime about 5.3x the register interpreter's CoreMark score (derived from page data, cross-run)
Picking the fastest interpreter: in the project's own chart wasm3 (2180.8) and stitch (2280.9) score at or above WasmKit 0.1.0 (2172.8)

Big-endian hosts (the C shim refuses to compile), or architectures outside x86, x86-64, ARM and AArch64, which get only the token-threaded fallback loop (its speed relative to direct threading is not documented)
Wasm GC modules (decoded but refused by the translator) or full WASI Preview 2/component model (in progress)
Functions whose frame exceeds the interpreter's operand reach: they are rejected with 'The frame of this function is too large for the interpreter'

integration.dependencies: none for the core engine (no Foundation, no external packages); swift-argument-parser and swift-syntax for the CLI and WIT tooling
integration.min_toolchain: Swift 6.3 (swift-tools-version 6.3, uses the experimental RawLayout feature); macOS 15 / iOS 18 deployment targets
integration.platforms: macOS 15+, iOS 18+, tvOS, watchOS, visionOS, Linux (Ubuntu 22.04+, Debian 12, Fedora 39+, Amazon Linux), Android API 30, Windows 10+, Embedded Swift bare metal; little-endian only; direct threading only on x86, x86-64, ARM, AArch64
integration.thread_safety: Engine is marked @unchecked Sendable (immutable configuration, synchronised type interner; not with interceptors); Store is thread-confined, and each WASI thread gets its own Store

gotchas: Harness flaw in the only quantified claim: the chart's WasmKit 0.0.8 bar (291.240274) and wasmi bar (1321.236383) are the exact figures from the earlier second-generation log, which already appears in PR #115 (merged 2024-08-14), while the 0.1.0 bar (2172.826551) comes from a later run on the 2024-09-17 snapshot; the 7.4x and the 1.64x-over-wasmi ratios are cross-run, and neither the wasmi version nor the wasm3/stitch builds are named (bench.py has no stitch engine).

The 'well competitive' sentence hides numbers: rasterising the chart SVG (labels are outlined glyphs) gives WasmKit 2172.8, wasm3 2180.8, stitch 2280.9, wasmi 1321.2, so WasmKit is 0.4% behind wasm3 and 4.7% behind stitch (derived from page data); it beats no external interpreter in the same run.

The .mprotect bounds-check mode installs process-wide SIGSEGV/SIGBUS handlers and reserves 4 GiB plus a guard tail of address space per wasm32 memory, yet the interpreter still runs checked loads and stores in that mode; .software avoids the signal handlers at little cost.

Default interpreter stack is 512 KB; deep recursion traps with 'call stack exhausted' until EngineConfiguration.stackSize is raised. Fuel metering is translation-time, so code translated without it cannot be budgeted later (overhead reported under 10% in issue #421).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick WasmKit over KinoWASM, wasman or DTVM when the host is Swift or Apple's JIT-free platforms and you want a SwiftPM dependency with no C/Rust toolchain; for raw interpreter speed in a C host KinoWASM's own CoreMark (4385.7 vs wasm3 3555.6) and wasm3 itself score higher, and DTVM is a JIT for a different speed class.
verified_claims_summary: First-party CoreMark (wasi-sdk clang 18.1.2 -O3) on a 2020 M1 Mac mini: the register interpreter (WasmKit 0.1.0, swift-DEVELOPMENT-SNAPSHOT-2024-09-17-a, swift build -c release) scored 2172.8 versus 291.2 for the 0.0.8 stack interpreter (7.46x, derived from page data), where the 291.2 comes from an earlier run; in the interpreter chart it trails wasm3 (2180.8) and stitch (2280.9) and leads a reused wasmi figure (1321.2).
status_note: Actively maintained (0.4.2 tagged 2026-10-11, community-maintained, bundled with Swift 6.2+ toolchains) and MIT-licensed except the Apache-2.0 GDB modules; usable today, but the only published performance numbers date from the 2024 0.1.0 interpreter and mix two runs, so treat it as a wasm3-class interpreter rather than a faster one.
